feature.title: The week ahead: a holiday-shortened test after the worst week in 18 months
body: **Monday:** US markets reopen after the S&P 500's 8.6% weekly loss, with futures bouncing about 1% to 2% overnight. The question is whether the gain holds at the open and whether volatility falls.

**Tuesday:** one preview lists Dell's earnings, with attention on AI-server orders and margins; I could not confirm the date. **Thursday:** US markets are closed for Thanksgiving. **Friday:** stocks end at 1:00 PM ET, and Black Friday is the first read on holiday spending.

**Beyond:** OPEC+ meets on Nov. 29, the Fed's decision is on Dec. 9, where a quarter-point hike was priced as near-certain, and the G20 in Miami on Dec. 14–15 is where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again.

stories.headline: Wall Street's worst week in over 18 months: S&P 500 falls 8.6%, Nasdaq 10% and turns negative for 2026
stories.dek: Final Friday closes: S&P 500 -3.7% to 6,910.39 for a seventh straight loss, Dow -1.9% to 48,147.33, Nasdaq -5.3% to 22,617.73. Thanksgiving week is the next test.
tldr: Friday's close: **S&P 500 -3.7% to 6,910.39** (seventh straight loss), **Dow -1.9% (-949.73) to 48,147.33**, **Nasdaq -5.3% to 22,617.73**, with the S&P 500 and Dow in a correction.
For the week: **S&P 500 -651.28 points (-8.6%)**, **Dow -4,200.22 (-8%)**, **Nasdaq -2,518.54 (-10%)**, the Russell 2000 -7.5%; the S&P 500 is still up about 0.9% for the year, the Nasdaq down 2.7%.
It is the S&P 500's worst week in more than 18 months, per an AP-style recap; I found no confirmed single cause, only reports tying it to AI stocks.
whatHappened: U.S. stocks ended a brutal week with another sharp drop. On Friday the S&P 500 fell about 3.7% to 6,910.39, its seventh straight loss, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 1.9%, or 949.73 points, to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.3% to 22,617.73. The Russell 2000 fell about 2.8% to 2,581.79. The S&P 500 and the Dow closed in a [[correction]], a fall of 10% or more from their records, and the Nasdaq erased its 2026 gain, per CNBC and an AP-style recap. These closes replace the preliminary Friday figures in the earlier edition, which were close but not exact.

For the week, from last Friday's closes, the S&P 500 lost 651.28 points, or 8.6%, the Dow lost 4,200.22 points, or 8%, the Nasdaq lost 2,518.54 points, or 10%, and the Russell 2000 lost about 7.5%. The recap called it the S&P 500's worst week in more than 18 months, and the Globe and Mail said all three indexes had their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025. Year to date, the S&P 500 is still up about 0.9%, the Dow up about 0.2%, and the Nasdaq down about 2.7%.
background: A week ago the S&P 500 sat at 7,561.67 after a strong rebound; it has now lost about 8.6% in five sessions and is roughly 11.6% below last month's record near 7,817. The Nasdaq's loss is larger because it is heavy in AI and mega-cap technology, and it has gone from a 2026 gain to a 2026 loss in a week.

The pattern matters for what comes next. A [[drawdown]] this fast is usually driven by forced selling by leveraged and systematic funds, which can overshoot, and then it either stabilizes or extends. Short weeks around Thanksgiving have thin liquidity, which can magnify moves in either direction.
whyItMatters: The market is down 8% to 10% in five sessions with the rate story still pointing up and the AI trade failing to rally on good news. Monday's open is the first test of whether the selling is exhausted. The things to watch are Nvidia and the AI leaders, volatility and credit spreads, and any change in tone from the Fed. I could not confirm a single cause for Friday's move, so I am not assigning one.

grandLine.title: A Sabaody bubble under pressure
grandLine.body: At Sabaody a coating of resin bubbles lets a ship dive deeper than it normally could, until the bubble pops under pressure. AI valuations played that role this year: they let the market go much deeper than earnings alone would carry it. This week the pressure came, and whether the bubble is only cracked or fully popped is what the next sessions will say.

views.thesis: A forced, one-way selloff like this tends to mark a tradeable low.
views.argument: Seven straight S&P 500 losses, a 10% Nasdaq weekly drop and a full correction in a month are signs of exhaustion, and the year-to-date gain for the S&P 500 is still positive. Nvidia's results were strong, so earnings have not deteriorated.

views.camp: The start of a bigger unwind
views.thesis: Fast corrections from record highs can become bear markets.
views.argument: The AI trade is breaking, rate hikes are still coming, and there is no obvious catalyst to turn the market. A holiday week with thin liquidity can speed declines, and stops can feed on themselves.

interview.question: The S&P 500 lost 8.6% this week and the Nasdaq turned negative for the year. What do you do on Monday?
interview.answer: I'd keep risk small and wait for confirmation. A move this fast and this broad looks like forced selling, which can overshoot, so I wouldn't short the low, but I also wouldn't try to catch it before I see a stabilizing day on falling volatility. I'd watch the VIX, credit spreads and how Nvidia holds a bounce. What would change my mind is a reversal on broad participation, which would say the selling is done, or a break to new lows on rising yields, which would say it is not.

followUp.question: Why does breadth matter after a drop like this?
followUp.answer: When most stocks fall together, the selling is across the market rather than one sector, which points to de-risking and not rotation. A rebound is more durable when most stocks participate.

trade.expression: Long an equal-weight S&P 500 ETF, short the Nasdaq-100, sized to the same dollar exposure
trade.rationale: If the AI unwind continues, the Nasdaq-100 is more concentrated in the affected names than the equal-weight index, so the long leg falls less. It also hedges overall market direction.
risks: A sharp AI-led rebound makes the Nasdaq-100 leg outperform and the pair loses.
Correlations rise in a crash, so both legs can fall together.

keyTerms.definition: A fall of 10% or more from a recent peak. A fall of 5% to 10% is usually called a pullback, and 20% a bear market.
keyTerms.example: The S&P 500 and Dow closed Friday in a correction.

keyTerms.definition: The fall in an asset or portfolio from its previous peak to its latest low, usually quoted as a percentage.
keyTerms.example: The S&P 500's drawdown is about 11.6% from last month's record.

watchNext.what: Whether the selling continues at the open or stabilizes; volatility and credit spreads.

stories.headline: Wall Street heads into a holiday-shortened week with volatility surging after its worst week in 18 months
stories.dek: Markets reopen Monday, close Thursday for Thanksgiving and end Friday's session at 1 p.m. ET. Anthropic shares also fell sharply after their debut.
tldr: Markets reopen Monday after the S&P 500's 8.6% weekly loss; they are closed Thursday, Nov. 26, and Friday, Nov. 27, ends at **1:00 PM ET**.
One report says the VIX nearly doubled to about **37** on Friday and the Dow closed below 50,000 for a second straight day.
Reports tie the drop to a mix of Nvidia's leadership and SEC troubles, a hawkish Fed and doubts about data-center spending; Anthropic fell sharply after its debut.
whatHappened: Wall Street ends a brutal week with investors asking whether the AI-led drop is a temporary correction after excessive enthusiasm or the start of a longer unwind. Coverage from NPR, Longbridge and TipRanks says several pressures hit at once: Nvidia's leadership crisis and reported SEC scrutiny, a hawkish Federal Reserve, and doubts about data-center spending. One report said the [[VIX]], Wall Street's fear gauge, nearly doubled to about 37 on Friday, and another said the Dow closed below 50,000 for a second straight day.

The calendar is short. U.S. markets are closed on Thursday, Nov. 26, for Thanksgiving and close at 1:00 PM ET on Friday, Nov. 27. One preview lists Dell's earnings on Tuesday, with attention on AI-server orders and margins, and inflation data and Black Friday retail spending as other reads this week; I could not confirm exact release dates. NPR's interviewee noted that thin holiday trading can make moves jerky. Schwab's market update was headlined 'Tech carnage continues, with Anthropic now falling,' and one report noted an early 10% drop in Anthropic's stock on Friday after its debut; I did not find its Friday close.
background: The week combined a rate story and an AI story. The Fed's October minutes were read as hawkish, with a December hike priced as near-certain, and the AI leaders could not rally on good news. When both drivers point the same way, selling can feed on itself.
Holiday weeks have lower volume, so the same order flow moves prices more. That cuts both ways: a bounce can overshoot as easily as a drop.
whyItMatters: Monday's open is the first test of whether the selling is exhausted. If volatility falls and breadth improves, a relief rally into the holiday is possible, and a washout would be called [[capitulation]]; if the VIX stays near 37 and the S&P 500 breaks lower, forced selling can continue into a thin session. I would not assume either outcome.

grandLine.title: The Calm Belt
grandLine.body: The Calm Belt has no wind, and ships stall dead in the water, surrounded by Sea Kings. A holiday week can feel like that: low volume, no clear trend, and sudden moves when something big surfaces. The danger is not the stillness but what comes up from below when no one can sail away.

views.thesis: Fear is high and selling looks forced, so the bias is to rebound.
views.argument: A VIX near 37, seven straight S&P 500 losses and a 10% Nasdaq weekly drop are the kind of extremes that often precede rebounds. The S&P 500 is still up for the year.

views.camp: A regime change in risk appetite
views.thesis: With rates and AI both pressuring stocks, there is no obvious catalyst to turn.
views.argument: Thin liquidity can speed declines, Nvidia faces regulatory questions, and the Fed is still tightening. Bounces in a holiday week may fail.

interview.question: The VIX is near 37 and markets reopen after the worst week in 18 months. How do you position for Monday?
interview.answer: I'd keep position sizes small and wait for confirmation. A VIX this high says options are expensive, so I'd rather use defined-risk structures than naked directional bets. I'd watch whether volatility falls at the open, how Nvidia and the AI leaders trade, and credit spreads. What would change my mind is a broad reversal with falling volatility, which would say the selling is exhausted, or a break to new lows on rising yields.

followUp.question: What does a high VIX tell you?
followUp.answer: It measures the cost of S&P 500 options, which is the market's expected volatility over the next 30 days. A spike means investors are paying up for protection, which is often seen near selling extremes, though it can stay high.

trade.idea: Sell premium into elevated volatility, defined risk
trade.expression: Sell a one-month S&P 500 put spread, short a put about 8% out of the money and long a put about 12% out of the money
trade.rationale: With the VIX near 37, option premium is rich. If the market stabilizes, the spread expires worthless and the seller keeps the premium, with the long put capping the loss.
risks: A further sharp drop through the short strike produces losses up to the width of the spread.
Volatility can rise further before it falls, so the position can show losses early.

keyTerms.definition: The CBOE index of expected 30-day volatility in the S&P 500, backed out of option prices. Often called the fear gauge; it rises when investors pay up for protection.
keyTerms.example: One report put it near 37 on Friday, nearly double its level a week earlier.

keyTerms.definition: A wave of panic selling that exhausts the sellers and often marks a low, though it is only clear in hindsight.
keyTerms.example: Traders will ask on Monday whether Friday's drop was capitulation.

watchNext.what: Whether volatility falls and breadth improves at the open.
Early close after Thanksgiving, with Black Friday as a read on consumers.

stories.headline: Trump and Xi meet in Shenzhen and reportedly agree to draft a 'strategic stability' plan; analysts call it modest
stories.dek: China's foreign ministry said the leaders met Thursday afternoon. Xi urged Trump to avoid setbacks on Taiwan, and Trump pressed China on U.S. farm purchases.
tldr: Xi and Trump met in Shenzhen on the afternoon of Nov. 19, on the sidelines of APEC, per China's foreign ministry.
They reportedly agreed to draw up an action plan for a relationship of strategic stability; a CFR analysis called the outcomes far more modest than the buildup suggested.
whatHappened: China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Xi met Trump in Shenzhen on the afternoon of Nov. 19 during the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting. Brasil de Fato reported that the two leaders agreed to formulate an action plan to build a bilateral relationship of strategic stability, and that Xi said ties were stable and improved. Reports said Xi urged Trump to avoid setbacks on Taiwan, and SCMP said Trump asked China to do more for U.S. farmers. A CFR analysis described the outcomes as far more modest than the buildup suggested. I found no announced new tariff or chip-export decisions; the trade truce already runs to January 10.
whyItMatters: With no new trade deliverables, the meeting reads as a holding pattern: the truce stays, and the larger decisions wait for the G20 in Miami on Dec. 14–15. The market relevance is the absence of a negative surprise on chips, tariffs or Taiwan during a week when AI stocks fell.

stories.headline: WSJ reports the SEC has opened a civil investigation into Nvidia's disclosures; neither Nvidia nor the SEC has confirmed
stories.dek: The probe follows Jensen Huang's Nov. 12 resignation as CEO, per reports. A civil probe is fact-finding and does not by itself establish wrongdoing.
tldr: The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 17, citing people familiar, that the SEC opened a civil investigation including whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors.
The SEC said only that it does not comment on the existence of a possible investigation; I found no public response from Nvidia.
whatHappened: The WSJ reported on Nov. 17 that the SEC has opened a civil investigation into Nvidia, including whether its disclosures gave investors an accurate picture of its business; the precise focus is unclear, per PYMNTS and InvestmentNews coverage. The report follows Huang's Nov. 12 resignation as CEO. Nvidia settled an earlier SEC disclosure matter in 2022 for $5.5 million, about crypto-mining's effect on its gaming revenue. Other outlets say shares fell more than 10% after Huang's exit and that a shareholder lawsuit cites earlier company statements. These details are reported, not confirmed.
whyItMatters: Regulatory overhang gives investors a reason to demand a bigger discount on the AI leader, and it was part of the mix of pressures that hit the Nasdaq this week. A civil probe can take months and often ends in a settlement, so the headline risk lasts longer than any one trading session.

stories.headline: US stock futures bounce after the AI rout as Asia braces for losses and Japan sits out a holiday
stories.dek: Nasdaq 100 futures rose about 2% early Monday and S&P 500 futures 1% to 2%, reports differ. Asian authorities reportedly stepped in to steady markets.
tldr: Early Monday, Nasdaq 100 futures were up about **2%** and S&P 500 futures about **1% to 2%**, depending on the report, after Friday's rout.
Japan's markets were closed for a holiday after the Nikkei fell **5.1%** on Friday; Hang Seng futures pointed lower.
One report says China cut its margin requirement, state funds bought record ETFs and South Korea readied a market stabilization fund.
whatHappened: U.S. stock [[futures]] rebounded early Monday after the sell-off that took the S&P 500 down 8.6% last week. The Star reported that Nasdaq 100 futures rose about 2% and S&P 500 futures about 1%; a second report put the S&P 500 futures gain nearer 2%, so the size of the bounce differs by source. Both tie it to Friday's rout in AI-related shares.

In Asia, Japanese markets were closed on Monday for a public holiday after the Nikkei 225 fell 5.1% on Friday, and Hang Seng futures pointed lower. One report said Chinese authorities cut the margin requirement and state funds bought a record amount of ETFs, and that South Korea prepared a market stabilization fund; I could not confirm these from a second outlet. The same report said the Nasdaq's 10% weekly drop was its steepest since March 2020.
background: A futures bounce after a sharp drop is common because positioning is light and sellers pause over a weekend. It is only a signal about the open, not the close: the gain has to survive the first hour and the rest of the day.

The Asian policy steps matter for sentiment. When authorities in China and South Korea step in to steady markets, it is a sign they see the drop as disorderly, which can help stop a spiral in their own markets, though it does not fix the underlying AI worries.
whyItMatters: This is the first session after the worst week in 18 months, so the open decides the tone for a short holiday week. A bounce that holds and comes with falling volatility would support the case for stabilization. A bounce that fades by midday would look like a [[dead-cat bounce]] and point to more selling into Thanksgiving.

grandLine.title: Knock Up Stream
grandLine.body: Knock Up Stream is a violent upward geyser at Jaya: the Going Merry rode it to Skypiea, but with bad timing the ship is destroyed. A sudden overnight gap up is like that. It can launch a rebound, but the timing has to be right, and it can wreck anyone who chases it at the top.

views.thesis: The bounce plus policy support in Asia marks an exhaustion of selling.
views.argument: After seven straight S&P 500 losses and a 10% Nasdaq week, positioning is light, authorities are stepping in, and good earnings from Nvidia haven't changed. A broad rebound with falling volatility would confirm it.

views.thesis: Overnight gaps in a downtrend usually fade.
views.argument: The drivers are still there: the Fed is tightening, Nvidia faces an SEC probe report, and AI spending doubts remain. A bounce into a thin holiday week can fail quickly.

interview.question: US futures are up about 2% after the worst week in 18 months. Do you buy the open?
interview.answer: I'd wait for the first hour. A futures bounce after a drop like this is expected, so the information is in whether it holds as cash markets open and whether volatility falls with it. I'd watch breadth, the VIX and Nvidia. What would change my mind is a sustained hold of the gains with broad participation, which says stabilization, or a fade to the lows by midday, which says the bounce was only positioning.

followUp.question: What is a dead-cat bounce?
followUp.answer: A short recovery in a falling market that fails and is followed by new lows. The name comes from the idea that even a dead cat will bounce if it falls from a great height.

keyTerms.definition: Contracts that track an index's expected level; they trade nearly around the clock and are used as an early read before the stock market opens.
keyTerms.example: Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 2% early Monday.

keyTerms.definition: A brief recovery in a falling market that fails, after which prices make new lows.
keyTerms.example: Traders will test whether Monday's gap up holds or fades.

watchNext.what: Whether the futures gains hold through the open and the first hour.
